name: Development Board

claims.claim_text: Do not design a manufacturer's development board into a product. It will not be purchasable in a year, because the board exists to sell silicon and is retired whenever that purpose is served.
claims.quote_verbatim: you won't be able to buy it in a year's time, I guarantee it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Op amps, Microchips & Mergers - Narquois Nerd Nescience - Narquois Nerd Nescience

claims.claim_text: Open sourcing the board does not solve that. If the vendor stops selling it you must manufacture it yourself, which removes the entire reason for using a vendor board, namely that anyone can simply buy one.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you'd have to go out and manufacture it yourself
claims.episode_title: Op amps, Microchips & Mergers - Narquois Nerd Nescience - Narquois Nerd Nescience

claims.claim_text: The vendor's reason for discouraging design-in is supply, not spite. A vendor plans a run sized for thousands of individual engineers; one customer designing the board into a product buys out that supply and the boards never reach the engineers they were made for.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're just going to design 4,000 of these into our product

claims.claim_text: Development boards carry deliberately lower profit margin than production boards and are frequently booked internally as a marketing expense rather than a product line. That accounting is why they are cheap and why the vendor does not want them becoming a revenue-bearing product.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do give your dev boards a lower profit margin than your production boards
claims.speaker: Elecia White

claims.claim_text: High evaluation-board pricing is often a deliberate filter rather than a margin. A board priced at $500 or $1,000 may cost $100 or $200 to build, and the premium exists to discourage tire-kickers, because supporting a hobbyist buyer can cost more than the board ever earns.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're trying to discourage, you know, what you might call the tire kickers
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Evaluation boards for silicon that is not aimed at the mass market never reach distributor catalogues at all. If you cannot find a board for a part, that is information about who the part is sold to.
claims.quote_verbatim: then there's no point in releasing the development kit to the mass market
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Microcontroller vendors compete on development-tool shipment counts and report them prominently in annual financial statements. Boards are given away so the number looks good, which is a large part of why so many end up unused in drawers.
claims.quote_verbatim: how many development tools they're shipped this year
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Actual utilisation is very low. Estimates from people who make and buy them put meaningful use in the single-digit percentages, with more than half being powered on once to run the demo application and then set aside.
claims.quote_verbatim: only single digit percentages end up being, you know, used

claims.claim_text: The counterweight to that waste is capability: because the ecosystem exists, almost any job has a board or module that will do it, which repeatedly rescues consulting schedules. The unused boxes of boards are what pays for that availability.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to get a job done, right, there's a dev board or, you know, some sort of module out there to do it

claims.claim_text: The build-versus-buy arithmetic rarely favours building. Assuming the parts are on hand, a milling machine is available and nothing is fine-pitch, the layout, assembly, testing and software still come to around thirty hours; at fifty dollars an hour that is $1,500, which buys six boards delivered overnight.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just said it was like 30 hours, and I said even at 50 bucks, that's, you know, that's $1,500

claims.claim_text: The bias to watch in yourself is wanting to build it because building is enjoyable and feels like the proper thing to do. Most of the time that is not the right call.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the time, that's not the right call

claims.claim_text: A part family of ten devices may have a board for only one of them, and that is usually enough. Most of the functionality can be evaluated on the single available board, with the footprint changed later for whichever family member the application needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: there might be 10 parts in a family and there's only one part that has a dev board
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: Keep your own board's pin assignment close to the vendor board's and you can reuse its build configuration wholesale. Putting the SD card on the same pins as the reference design means the existing config files simply work.
claims.quote_verbatim: as long as you make your board kind of similar to EVK, you can basically just steal their dev configs

claims.claim_text: The general rule behind that is not to move pins without a reason, because the reference board remains a live sanity check. When your board misbehaves you can probe the same point on both and see immediately that one is high and the other low.
claims.quote_verbatim: why did you move this pin?

claims.claim_text: What makes a genuinely useful development board is unglamorous: every pin brought out to 0.1 inch headers. Most of these parts have no exotic high-speed peripherals demanding special connectors, so the specialised interface boards vendors prefer add cost without adding access.
claims.quote_verbatim: what I want to see is dev boards with 0.1 inch headers for every pen

claims.claim_text: Vendor boards are frequently poor enough that experienced engineers build their own breakouts rather than use them, particularly when a vendor adopts a fashionable form factor instead of exposing the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: the dev boards are quite crappy

claims.claim_text: A good cheap FPGA board contains only what is needed: the FPGA, its regulators, a JTAG programmer, and every pin on headers. Around seventeen pounds buys that, and nothing else on the board is missed.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got the FPGA, voltage regs, JTAG programmer, and all the pins broken out onto headers
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The part choice that makes such a board possible is on-chip flash, on-chip regulator and on-chip oscillator, which removes most support circuitry. The trade is packaging: the small QFN version drops the memory blocks and PLLs, so needing those forces a hundred-pin package.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got on-chip flash, on-chip regulator, and on-chip oscillator
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The board itself is rarely the innovation. Boards of this kind had existed for decades before the popular ones arrived; what distinguishes them is the integrated development environment and the critical mass of users around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the IDE that makes the Arduino
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: Stated the other way: strip away the ecosystem and community and what remains is another development board. The hook that creates the community is being able to impart a change on the physical world, starting with a blinking LED.
claims.quote_verbatim: otherwise the Arduino is just yet another development board
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: The same argument applies to single-board computers. Without the community and software around it, the object is just a single-board computer, and industrial catalogues have carried those since the 1970s.
claims.quote_verbatim: otherwise it's just a single board computer you can get
claims.episode_title: Hyperloop, Upverter and Soldering - Unbelievable USB Ustulater

claims.claim_text: The economics that changed everything: two decades ago the chip alone might be thirty dollars, the development environment another thousand, and the board five hundred, so nobody had them lying around to experiment with. Boards now cost a few dollars, which is what made casual experimentation possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: the development board would be 500 bucks a pop
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: Before low-cost interpreter boards existed, every demo board came from a manufacturer, was aimed at professionals and cost hundreds of dollars. The shift was as much about who was permitted to buy one as about the price.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the demo boards were from the manufacturers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: A cautionary case in board pricing: a $4,000 development board built on the premise that plugging pre-made modules together would remove the need to design custom boards at all, sold with a software licence that pointedly excluded the PCB tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the whole idea was that you could plug these modules into your product

claims.claim_text: It did not sell. Distributors returned their stock and the product had to be bought back, which is what a board priced above what the market will bear looks like from the inside.
claims.quote_verbatim: it priced itself out of the market

claims.claim_text: The correction was an order-of-magnitude price cut: a $300 successor compatible with the same modules, which sold far better. Same technology, different price, entirely different outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: which sold, which sold a lot better
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: The technology in the expensive version was genuinely advanced, with modules auto-detected over one-wire serial numbers and the corresponding FPGA configuration pulled in automatically. Capability was never the problem, which is the point worth remembering.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could actually plug in the modules and it'd auto detect them via one wire serial numbers
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: The reference point that shows how far board pricing fell: vendor discovery boards at nine dollars. Any board priced in the hundreds now competes against that expectation.
claims.quote_verbatim: discovery boards at $9 are the dev boards
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Boards at seventy-five to a hundred dollars are still too expensive for a university course, because the cost multiplies by the number of students. Educational use has a different price ceiling than professional evaluation.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're still 75 to a hundred bucks
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres

claims.claim_text: At the hobbyist end, a $130 board simply to gain access to a processor reads as steep, which shapes which parts get tried by people who are not spending an employer's money.
claims.quote_verbatim: $130 dev board to just have access to the processor is steep
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman

claims.claim_text: Vendor evaluation boards are designed to illustrate every function and feature of the silicon to a working engineer. Making teaching or learning easier is a different goal producing a different board, and confusing the two leads to disappointment with both.
claims.quote_verbatim: their goal was to illustrate all the functions and features of a given piece of silicon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Sponsored ecosystem solutions create a false sense of security. The pre-selected boards and software stack give a genuine head start, but the moment you need a neighbouring part number or your own processor you are back in green-field territory with none of the support.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you don't, if you want to, if you want to, you know, integrate your one special thing or use that really unique processor, well, good luck

claims.claim_text: The specific trap that costs schedules: prove the concept on the vendor board, get approval on the strength of it, then have purchasing or a memory requirement force a different part, at which point the work restarts and the timeline needs months added.
claims.quote_verbatim: And now it's a totally different part

claims.claim_text: The corresponding advice is to commit or not commit, but not to half-commit: if you are going to buy into a vendor's ecosystem, buy all the way in, and expect to be charged somewhere on the back end because that is the business the ecosystem exists to support.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're going to buy in, buy all the way in

claims.claim_text: Building a product on a complete board inherits its entire bill of materials as a supply risk. A hundred-line product bill can be engineered with substitutes; a board that itself depends on two hundred parts is a single bottleneck you cannot substitute around.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's a big bottleneck in the chain potential bottleneck

claims.claim_text: At volume the move is to buy the silicon and negotiate directly with the chip vendor rather than buying finished boards, keeping the software stack while getting the price that comes from being a significant customer. Selling chips is what the board programme was for anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might have to go and talk to the vendor directly

claims.claim_text: Cloning a board's pinout is good for the industry rather than a threat to it. A market where every board has a different interface serves nobody, and attempts to protect a product at the interface layer would be a bad sign for everyone.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want every single development board on the market to have a different bloody interface
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: The argument for placing development and breakout boards in the public domain rather than under a share-alike licence: the board exists specifically for an engineer to learn from or build on, so restricting it is self-defeating, like a textbook demanding attribution each time you use a formula.
claims.quote_verbatim: why on earth would you lock that down?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Design the first-cut board for measurement rather than for production. Jumpers to isolate sections and small current shunts in the supply rails let you meter each part of the circuit directly instead of cutting traces later.
claims.quote_verbatim: It'll even have little current shunts in there so that you can put your current meter in there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: Getting-started guides remain unreliable, and the eventual cause is often mundane rather than technical: one multi-day debugging session ended when the board turned out to be a different part in a mislabelled bag. Read the part number on the silicon before trusting the packaging.
claims.quote_verbatim: the board was labeled in the wrong bag

claims.claim_text: The accompanying human failure is assuming the fault must be yours and then changing far too many things at once, which destroys the ability to tell which change mattered.
claims.quote_verbatim: trying way too many things, honestly

claims.claim_text: Vendor tool installations are enormous because a single installer covers every board in the range plus every analysis tool, rather than the one board you actually own. There is usually no way to install support for just your hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: they support, like, 30 different boards in one install
claims.episode_title: Silego, ADCs & Seismic Detection - Dave's Dingo Dystocia

claims.claim_text: The modern fast-prototype pattern: take a vendor board off the shelf, design only the custom sensor board, connect through the board's standard header, add a display and a 3D-printed case. The result costs perhaps ten to twenty times a production version and exists in a fraction of the time.
claims.quote_verbatim: I took a dev board off the shelf. I made a sensor board that was custom for my application

claims.claim_text: The economics that made that pattern sensible: for one-off and small quantities, material cost used to rival the engineering cost. Materials are now cheap while engineering time is not, which shifts the decision decisively toward assembling from existing boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of material is, is so cheap and NREs is still expensive

claims.claim_text: Before standard stacking connectors existed, a quick prototype meant buying a vendor microcontroller board, a separate sensor board from a different vendor, and wiring them into a fragile assembly, with each board around fifty dollars and rarely carrying the sensor you actually wanted.
claims.quote_verbatim: you had to get a bunch of development boards

claims.claim_text: The step that matters in learning is moving off the board onto your own design, and what it requires is datasheet literacy: which decoupling capacitors are needed, which pins need pull-ups, what the boot mode pins do. That knowledge is what replaces header connections that work loose.
claims.quote_verbatim: What does this boot mode pin do?
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Copying vendor reference schematics is legitimate practice, not cheating, and you will still make mistakes doing it. Those mistakes are where the learning actually happens.
claims.quote_verbatim: you copy it and you're still going to mess stuff up just because you're copying it
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: The silicon-design equivalent of starting from a development board is a proven, tested chip published together with its board, so a designer can clone the whole thing and replace only their own block, keeping the rest of the chip and its verification benches intact.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can use the rest of the chip just by unplugging that and putting that, putting mine
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Build your own evaluation board when the vendor's breakout does not support the work. A breakout with nowhere to attach a scope probe or a jumper is not an evaluation platform, and the replacement saves time for everyone who evaluates that part afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was nowhere I can hook up my oscilloscope
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: One artefact can serve three roles simultaneously: a castellated module you solder down, a reference design to copy, and a development board to work on. Keeping it simple and cheap covers the high-volume case and leaves fuller-featured variants to third parties.
claims.quote_verbatim: Pico is both, uh, a module that you can solder in yourself and a reference design and, and just, and a dev board
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: The same object is classified differently by different audiences, and both classifications are correct: electronics people saw a development board while consumers saw a computer. Which one it is determines the compliance expectations it must meet.
claims.quote_verbatim: we viewed it as a dev board
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: Many boards on the market carry no CE or FCC marking, and at small volume the risk is often absorbed. That option disappears when a product has public visibility as a high-volume item before a single unit ships, at which point compliance has to be taken seriously from the start.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are a lot of boards out there that aren't C marks, aren't FCC clear
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: A board vendor's reason not to support a second FPGA family: the two families offer no capability difference that matters to most users, so a second board doubles the support burden while doubling nothing else. What changes the calculation is the silicon vendor offering a discount to get a board into the market.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm just going to be supporting twice as my stuff without getting twice as many different capabilities
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: A sensible two-tier board strategy pairs a simple entry board with an easily understood feature set against a full-feature board that breaks out everything on the module, so the second one supports current measurement and deeper testing that the first deliberately hides.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can test anything on the module with, with this dev board
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: Cost-reduced boards fail in a particular way: built to a price with no attention beyond the first power-on, they get used once and discarded, which is a different problem from being merely inexpensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: they turn them once, and then they throw them away

claims.claim_text: There are designs where a general-purpose board is simply the wrong tool. Anything constrained on size and weight, an airborne platform being the standard example, needs a custom board carrying the minimum circuitry required to do the job.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't use a bloody Arduino

claims.claim_text: A recurring dispute in education is whether using a ready-made board counts as cheating when the board is a means to an end rather than the subject of the project. The answer depends on what is being assessed, which is worth stating in the brief rather than leaving implicit.
claims.quote_verbatim: they used it as a means to an end
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: Claims that a conference badge will be reused afterwards as a development board are almost never borne out, even when the hardware would genuinely support it, with a large FPGA still well under half utilised after everything the badge itself does.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll use the conference badge as a dev board

claims.claim_text: Cheap consumer devices make good development hardware when the microcontroller inside can be reprogrammed, since they package a processor and radio in a finished enclosure and often expose test points. Small trackers and tags are the standard example.
claims.quote_verbatim: They make really nice dev boards
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: A persistent gap in the board market is a display built onto the board itself rather than stacked on as a daughterboard. Boards that do integrate one, some around fifteen dollars with a small OLED, a wireless processor and a long-range radio, are unusually useful for that reason alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: not a hat, not a daughter board that goes on top, but a, but an actual one that's built on
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
